Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

These cues imply military/combat and sexual-threat or specific geopolitical associations that are not plausibly linked to the reported trauma, and no accompanying threat, appraisal, or strategy items provide a bridge that would make these triggers understandable for this patient. By contrast, the memory items are internally coherent and fit severe reliving after an MVC, as well as the active Memory → Triggers formulation.

'Cars hit by accident' fits the trauma and aligns with the active Memory → Triggers formulation, but 'Sexual situations or intimacy' and 'Arab villages' imply very different trauma contexts (e.g., sexual trauma or combat/terrorism-related threat) that are not represented anywhere else in Memory, Threat, Appraisals, or Strategies. This makes the trigger profile hard to explain as belonging to the same patient and trauma.

For a 51-year-old male welder whose index trauma is a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, the trigger 'Arab villages' is hard to reconcile clinically with the stated trauma type and the rest of the profile. The memory items all concern vivid sensory/bodily reliving of a crash, which coheres with MVC trauma and the active Memory → Triggers edge, but 'Arab villages' implies a war-zone or ethnopolitical context that is not represented anywhere else in the self-report or formulation. This is a clearly implausible trigger for this trauma profile, unlike the crash imagery and alcohol smell triggers, which could plausibly cue MVC memories.

vignette:
Keanu remembers the rain. Not just the sight of it, but the percussive sound on the roof of his Ford F-150, a steady drumming that had almost lulled him into a sense of calm on the drive home from the shop six months ago. The intersection was slick with it. He recalls the green light, the smell of the damp upholstery, and then the sudden, violent intrusion of headlights from his left. The screech of tires was instantly devoured by the deafening crunch of metal. In the moments before he blacked out, two things seared themselves into his mind: the sight of the other driver's face, slack and surprised behind a spiderweb of shattered glass, and the overwhelming, sweet-sick stench of whiskey that flooded his cab when the first responders pulled the man from the wreckage. The impact had thrown him against the driver's side door, his left leg pinned and his chest crushed against the steering wheel, a searing, electric pain that he thought was the end of everything.

Now, at fifty-one, Keanu's world is circumscribed by the echoes of that moment. The memories are not memories in the typical sense; they are invasions. Last week, while walking to the local market, he saw a minor fender-bender at a stop sign. The sight of the crumpled bumper was a key turning a lock in his mind. Instantly, he was no longer on the sidewalk but back in his truck. The smell of rain-soaked asphalt filled his nostrils, the phantom stench of whiskey burned his throat, and the ghost of the steering wheel pressed into his ribs, stealing his breath. His body, betraying the solid ground beneath his feet, contorted involuntarily. His left leg seized with a blinding, remembered agony, and his torso twisted hard to the right, a physical reenactment of the crash that left him staggering against a wall, gasping for air that felt thick with gasoline fumes.

His work as a welder, once a source of pride and stability, has become a landscape of potential threats. The shop is on a busy industrial road, and the sound of a truck downshifting or the sudden squeal of brakes from the street outside can send a jolt of pure terror through him. He finds himself bracing for an impact that never comes, his muscles coiling tight. More than once, he has dropped a tool, his focus shattered by a passing car. His colleagues have noticed his jumpiness, the way he flinches at loud noises. He's started wearing heavy-duty ear protectors even when he's not actively welding, trying to build a wall of silence against the world, but it only makes him feel more isolated.

Life at home has changed in subtle, corrosive ways. His wife, Leilani, now does all the driving. Keanu hasn't touched the keys to his new truck since they bought it. The thought of being behind the wheel, of being responsible for their safety, is unbearable. He used to love their big family barbecues, but a few months ago, his cousin opened a beer near him, and the faint smell of alcohol sent him spiraling. He felt the phantom pain flare in his leg so intensely he had to limp away, making an excuse about an old work injury. He saw the confusion in Leilani's eyes. He knows she doesn't understand why he is pulling away, why the man she married seems to be fading, replaced by someone perpetually on edge. He has come to believe his body is fundamentally broken, that the pain from the accident is a permanent part of him, ready to surge back to life without warning.

It was a conversation with his foreman last week that finally pushed him to seek help. After another near-miss with a piece of equipment, his boss told him, kindly but firmly, that he needed to get himself sorted out before he seriously hurt himself or someone else. Keanu sat in his truck in the parking lot-a passenger, as always-and felt a profound sense of despair. He is trapped in a cycle he cannot break, his own body a constant reminder of the moment he nearly died. He is not hoping for a miracle; his hopes are much smaller, more vital. He just wants to be able to sit in a car without his muscles clenching in remembered pain, to smell a beer at a cookout without reliving a nightmare, and to feel, for the first time in six months, that he is living in the present, not in the wreckage of the past.
